messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: stringstream and Scientific Notation
parts:
I tracked down the bug in bin/print, and it occurs when string stream tries to parse a number in scientific notation with three digits in the exponent, for example "ss >> 1.78358e-321".  The stream fails, and then further uses of operator>> read from random memory, hence the incorrect results.

This looks like a bug in stringstream (two digits in the exponent parses just fine) -- does anyone have any problem with my thresholding values in mcmc_writer?  Basically anything below 1e-50 would be set to zero.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stringstream and Scientific Notation
parts:
Curious. The number is between min() and denorm_min() for doubles:

std::cout << "1.78358e-321=" << 1.78358e-321 << std::endl;
std::cout << "min=" << std::numeric_limits<double>::min() << std::endl;
std::cout << "denorm min=" << std::numeric_limits<double>::denorm_min() << std::endl;

prints:

1.78358e-321=1.78358e-321
min=2.22507e-308
denorm min=4.94066e-324

My go-to reference

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/limits/numeric_limits/

says min() is:

Minimum finite value.
For floating types with denormalization (variable number of exponent bits):
minimum positive normalized value.
Equivalent to CHAR_MIN, SCHAR_MIN, SHRT_MIN, INT_MIN, LONG_MIN, LLONG_MIN, FLT_MIN,
DBL_MIN, LDBL_MIN or 0, depending on type.

and for denorm_min(), it says:

Minimum positive denormalized value.
For types not allowing denormalized values: same as min().

I have no idea what denormalization is, but it looks relevant here.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stringstream and Scientific Notation
parts:
In IEEE floating point, the number is represented in two parts.  The base number and the exponent, i.e., 1.423566 x 10^-123 (except in base 2) where 1.423566 is the base and -123 is, obviously, the exponent.

There are a certain number of bits given to represent the base and the exponent.  Once the maximum value of the exponent has been reached, that is basically the min value.  However, you can get a slight more range by allowing the base number to be denormalized.  I.E., if you write 0.0000001 x 10^-123, that is a denormalied base.

I would be surprised if this is related to what is going on here.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stringstream and Scientific Notation
parts:
Yes. That's really lousy behavior. No idea what
the full spec is, so I don't know if it's a bug or if
input is undetermined after an error.

With:

std::stringstream ss;
double y1, y2;
std::string punct;
ss << "2.9e-200, 3.14";
ss >> y1 >> punct >> y2;
std::cout << "y1=" << y1 << "; y2=" << y2 << "; punct=" << punct << std::endl;

I get:

y1=2.9e-200; y2=3.14; punct=,

but with ss set to underflow,

ss << "2.9e-400, 3.14";

I get:

y1=0; y2=0; punct=

But then I tried first setting y1 and y2 and
noticed that in the error case you get no change to the variables.
So with

std::stringstream ss;
double y1 = 152, y2 = -3;
std::string punct;
ss << "2.9e-400, 3.14";
ss >> y1 >> punct >> y2;
std::cout << "y1=" << y1 << "; y2=" << y2 << "; punct=" << punct << std::endl;

I got:

y1=152; y2=-3; punct=

Same results under clang++ and g++ under -O1 and -O3 by the way.

- Bob
